questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code streams the uploaded photo to the object store? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
The handler wraps r.Body with http.MaxBytesReader instead of only rejecting requests whose Content-Length header is too large. Why is that more robust?
choices: MaxBytesReader compresses the body so less memory is needed
The header can be absent (chunked uploads) or wrong, whereas MaxBytesReader enforces the limit on the bytes actually read and returns an error once it is exceeded
MaxBytesReader validates that the body is a well-formed multipart message
Go refuses to parse multipart bodies unless MaxBytesReader is present

questions.prompt: Roughly how much memory does one in-flight upload need, as a function of the photo size?
choices: Proportional to the photo size, because the part is buffered before Put is called
Proportional to the photo size, because the hasher keeps all bytes it has seen
Constant, apart from the sniff buffer and I/O buffers, because the part is streamed through the hasher to the store
Zero, because the Go runtime spools request bodies to disk

questions.prompt: If Put fails midway, for example because the client disconnects, why does the cleanup use context.WithoutCancel(r.Context())?
choices: The request context is cancelled when the client goes away, so Delete would fail immediately and leave the partial object behind
WithoutCancel gives the delete a longer deadline than the upload
WithoutCancel makes Delete run in a separate goroutine
The store requires a fresh context for every call
